canberra.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft to cross invisible one ‘light day’ threshold in space
canberra.snippet: At about 9:16 pm Australian Eastern Daylight Time on Wednesday (18 November), a man-made object will cross an invisible threshold in spac...
canberra.content:
Concept art of Voyager 1 flying through interstellar space. Image: NASA.

At about 9:16 pm Australian Eastern Daylight Time on Wednesday (18 November), a man-made object will cross an invisible threshold in space that will place it more than one ‘light day’ away from Earth.

The Voyager 1 spacecraft was launched 49 years ago on 5 September 1977 from Cape Canaveral in the US, and is NASA’s longest running mission.

After conducting close flybys of Jupiter and Saturn and some of their moons in 1979 and 1980 respectively, it departed the known Solar System and crossed into interstellar space in August 2012. Since then, Voyager 1 has continued to fly away from the Sun at an astonishing speed of about 61,000 kilometres per hour.

That one light day distance is equivalent to 25.9 billion kilometres from Earth, but when you’re talking about numbers that large, it becomes easier to talk in the amount of time light takes to travel that distance – in this instance one day.

To put a light day into perspective, light travels at about 300,000 km per second, and radio signals travel at the speed of light in the vacuum of space.

The Moon is – on average – about 384,000 km from Earth, so light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel that distance. The Sun is 149.6 million kilometres (or 1 Astronomical Unit = AU) from Earth, so light from the Sun takes nearly eight and a half minutes to reach the Earth.

Neptune – the Solar System’s most outer planet – lies an average of about 4.5 billion kilometres or 4.18 light hours from the Sun, although its distance from Earth can be more or less depending on the two planets’ orbits.

Voyager 1 was launched by a Titan III rocket from Cape Canaveral on 5 September 1977. Photo: NASA.

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a ring of asteroids and rock fragments that extend from about 4 billion to 7.5 billion kilometres, or between 3.9 and nearly 7 light hours from the Sun.

Beyond the Kuiper Belt lies the heliopause – the point where scientists accept that interstellar space starts – at about 12 light hours from the Sun.

At more than 25.78 billion kilometres, or 172.39 AUs, or one light day, Voyager 1 is twice that distance from the Sun.

But despite having left the Solar System far behind, it is still a long way from reaching any more known heavenly bodies.

The next nearest star to Earth is Proxima Centauri which is 4.25 light years away. With Voyager 1 having taken more than 49 years to travel just one light day, it would take more than 75,000 years to reach the two planets so far discovered to be orbiting Proxima Centauri.

The Milky Way Galaxy is 100,000 light years in diameter, and is one of billions of galaxies that can be seen from Earth. The farthest object observed from Earth is the MoM-z14 galaxy which was observed by the James Webb Telescope (JWT) and which is estimated to be 33.8 billion light years away.

The Cosmic Microwave Background or ‘glow’ from the Big Bang which is thought to have created the universe forms what astronomers commonly call the cosmic horizon, and this is estimated to be 46.5 billion light years away, making the observable known universe at least 95 billion light years across.

Voyager 1’s mission was designed to last just five years, so its longevity has surprised even the most optimistic NASA engineers.

The 815 kilogram Voyager 1 was actually launched 16 days after sister-ship Voyager 2 which took a more scenic journey through the Solar System via Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Voyager 2 has also left the Solar System and is travelling away from the Sun at a more leisurely pace of just 54,900 kilometres per hour. It currently sits at about 144.5 AUs or 20 light hours and five light minutes away.

Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. Photos: NASA.

Canberra’s Deep Space Communications Complex at Tidbinbilla has played a key role in maintaining communications with the two Voyager spacecraft since they were launched. The CSIRO-run facility and its 70-metre steerable dish array – along with locations in California and Spain – allow NASA to monitor and maintain contact with the spacecraft at all times.

As technology advanced, remote-control reprogramming by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratories (JPL) has been used to upgrade the spacecraft’s software as the mission continued. This enabled the initial five-year mission to be extended to 12 years, and enabled Voyager 2 to be ‘diverted’ to visit Uranus and Neptune.

The spacecraft carry three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTG) – effectively mini nuclear batteries that convert the heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity – that produced at launch about 470 watts of power and which weighed about 150 kilograms.

NASA estimates the RTGs now produce less than 200 watts as they have shed about half their mass and passed the projected half-life of the fuel.

Because of the decay, NASA has switched off Voyager 1’s visual and radiological sensors, particle collectors, and some instruments in recent years.

The only active instruments left running are the spacecraft’s magnetometer which measures the strength and direction of magnetic fields, and its plasma wave subsystem which detects interactions between magnetic fields and charged particles.

NASA hopes this hibernation of the other system will allow the RTGs to continue to produce sufficient power for the spacecraft to return engineering data to Earth until 2036.

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: ACT Policing not investigating potential criminal charges in wake of Operation Kingfisher report
canberra.snippet: ACT Policing’s top cop has confirmed the force is not investigating whether to press several criminal charges in the wake of Operat...
canberra.content:
18 November 2026

Join the conversation

1

ACT Policing CPO Scott Lee confirmed his officers haven’t opened an investigation in the wake of Operation Kingfisher’s findings. Photo: Region.

ACT Policing’s top cop has confirmed the force is not investigating whether to press several criminal charges in the wake of Operation Kingfisher.

But Chief Police Officer Scott Lee said other prosecutorial avenues were available to the ACT Integrity Commission over the serious corrupt conduct findings against two former public servants.

The ACT Integrity Commission found former Education Directorate head Katy Haire had breached public trust by either misusing or abusing her authority, and that she’d engaged in deliberate acts of dishonesty.

It outlined Ms Haire’s serious corrupt conduct could constitute offences under the ACT’s Criminal Code, including general dishonesty, conspiracy to defraud, knowingly giving false or misleading information, producing false or misleading documents and abuse of public office.

The Integrity Commission also determined former Education Minister chief of staff Joshua Cermadis could be open to charges relating to conspiracy to defraud and abuse of public office.

CPO Lee said Integrity Commissioner Michael Adams KC had drawn Operation Kingfisher’s findings to his attention, but it wasn’t a referral to police.

“It was simply drawing that matter to our attention for consideration of any action we may take,” he said.

But ACT Policing has decided not to take the matter further.

“It is a very complex issue where you are looking at material that has been obtained through compellable hearings processes, so there is then a derivative use risk from that material that has implications for any investigation or prosecution,” CPO Lee said.

“[It was] a protracted investigation that took place over a number of years … it is an extremely complex undertaking then to try and consider that material in a way that can then be used for other processes.”

But this doesn’t mean a line has been drawn under the issue.

“In my view, if there is material that’s held by the Integrity Commission that goes to criminal offences, it is open to the Integrity Commission to also provide that material to the Director of Public Prosecutions to see whether there is sufficient material there for prosecution,” CPO Lee said.

The ACT Integrity Commission confirmed it had not referred the case to the DPP.

“The Integrity Commission is prohibited by the Integrity Commission Act 2018 from recommending prosecution for a criminal offence in an investigation report. As such, no recommendations have been made either to ACT Policing or the ACT Director of Public Prosecutions,” a spokesperson said.

“The question whether a prosecution should be undertaken is a matter for each entity to determine in accordance with their protocols. Such a decision rightly requires the exercise of a wholly independent discretion.”

Section 111 of the Integrity Commission Act 2018 does allow for the formal referral of matters to the DPP.

The ACT DPP does not have investigative powers, and matters are usually referred following police investigations.

Ms Haire resigned from her position in October 2024 — shortly after she dropped Supreme Court action against the Integrity Commission.

Mr Ceramidas was working for the Justice and Community Safety Directorate when the Operation Kingfisher findings were published.

He’s since left the ACT Public Service.

Mr Ceramidas currently has legal action against the ACT Integrity Commission afoot in Federal Court.

canberra.title: Hanson pledges deep cuts to refugee and parent visas as Labor and Coalition push back
canberra.snippet: One Nation will slash Australia’s refugee intake by 90 per cent and stop migrants relocating their parents to Australia, if the party fin...
canberra.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson wants to reduce Australia’s humanitarian refugee intake by 90 per cent. Photo: Facebook.

One Nation will slash Australia’s refugee intake by 90 per cent and stop migrants relocating their parents to Australia, if the party finds itself in any position of government after the next federal election.

Party leader Pauline Hanson has unveiled the second stage of her migration policy: reducing Australia’s humanitarian intake from 20,000 to 2000 places and scrapping the parent visa scheme.

The scheme currently allows about 7000 parents and grandparents of migrants to migrate to Australia each year.

In announcing her new policy platform in Parliament House on Wednesday (18 November), Senator Hanson said Australia could no longer afford the humanitarian or family migration schemes.

She acknowledged that the nation was built on migration, but she said it had gotten out of control and had become far too expensive for Australians to bear.

“The cost to the taxpayer is enormous,” Senator Hanson said.

“The cost is, on average, about $500,000 a year in a lifetime of expenditure per person in the country.

“We’ve got to take a tough stance on this. My concern is for these people out there that are doing it tough.

“You don’t bring more people into the country if they cannot fund their own bed or hospital beds.”

Parents of migrants currently on waiting lists or in Australia on bridging visas would have to take a refund and/or leave under a One Nation government.

About 150,000 people are in the queue for a parent visa.

Those already in Australia on bridging visas who want to stay would need to apply for a temporary sponsored parent visa, but “the families will have to pay for it”.

On the humanitarian intake side, the One Nation leader denied she was snubbing Australia’s international refugee obligations.

“What we’re looking at is humanitarian and those people coming here to stay in Australia,” she said.

“I’m not slamming the door shut at all. We’re saying 2000 people, that’s the limit.”

Foreign Minister Penny Wong described One Nation’s new policy as “very harsh” and said Australia’s refugee intake was not too high.

“There are countries which take more refugees [than Australia does]; there are countries which take fewer. We think this is the right balance,” Senator Wong said.

“When I deal with other countries, one of the things I talk about is who we are in Australia.

“Australia is an extraordinary country and a country which is informed by the richness of First Nations cultures and everyone who has arrived since.”

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said One Nation’s migration policy would inevitably lead to worker shortages in Australia’s hospital, aged care and construction sectors.

“Think about the hospital system. Half of the doctors on visas would not come,” he said.

“Half of the construction workers on visas would not come. It’s even worse for aged care workers and nurses.

“We can’t run our hospital system without visas. We can’t run our aged care system without visas.

“What One Nation is proposing is a complete attack on the services that Australians rely on.”

Mr Burke revealed new changes to Labor’s migration policy on Tuesday, backing down on some tough Working Holiday Maker (WHM) visa measures he announced just weeks ago.

The proposed cap on third-year visas under the flagged new ballot system will rise from 5000 to 25,000, but the number of days backpackers on WHM visas must serve in the regions to be eligible for a second year will increase from 88 to 120.

The minister defended the backflip on Wednesday, saying the significantly increased number of backpackers eligible for a third-year visa would provide “a bit more headspace”.

“It’s been a way to deliver what business needs, deliver what the regions need, while still delivering on the national expectation that we will manage the program in a way that matches the numbers that are in the budget,” he said.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor hasn’t embraced One Nation’s plan either, saying the Coalition has a better policy.

He said he wouldn’t be matching One Nation’s plan to reduce Australia’s humanitarian refugee intake to 2000 places.

“We’re going to oversee the biggest cuts to migration numbers in our country’s history to provide breathing space for housing in this country but to keep the skilled migration this country needs,” Mr Taylor said.

“Some of the greatest Australians came here as refugees – some of those who have built the most successful businesses – an extraordinary group of people.”

Last month, the Coalition vowed to reduce overseas migration numbers to 100,000 for two years and slash a massive 650,000 temporary visa holders over four years, if elected to government.

canberra.title: Parents ACT demands transparency as government refuses to name schools losing funding in 2027
canberra.snippet: Families are being left in the dark about what the 2027 public school budgets mean for their communities, Parents ACT says. The group rep...
canberra.content:
ACT Parents says it will be monitoring the school resourcing situation. Photo: ACT Public Schools.

Families are being left in the dark about what the 2027 public school budgets mean for their communities, Parents ACT says.

The group representing school P&Cs is calling on the ACT Government to publish comparative funding figures so parents can see whether their school is facing a cut.

It also wants the Education Directorate to provide school-specific information on what the ramifications are for communities.

ACT Parents Executive Officer Veronica Elliott said not providing such information would only put principals and school leaders under more pressure from parents wanting to know what was going to happen.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith announced the projected 2027 budgets on Tuesday (17 November) but would not name which schools would lose funding.

Ms Stephen-Smith said she did not want to expose principals to potential psychosocial harm by publishing a league table of schools.

But Ms Elliott said this would be counterproductive, saying parents deserved to know and the uncertainty would only drive them to ask more questions.

“We know that principals and school leaders have been under an enormous amount of pressure in recent weeks, providing information to the Education Directorate about the operation of their school and risk management,” she said.

“Not publishing information on the changes to the projected budget for 2027 in comparison with this year’s actual spending will probably lead to more people asking questions of their principal and looking for that information in other sources, and that possibly will have a negative impact on the psychosocial safety of our principals and school leaders.”

Ms Elliott said principals should not be left carrying the can for the changes when the Directorate should be the one explaining them to parents.

Parents ACT Executive Officer Veronica Elliott says the true cost of running a school and meeting student needs was still not known. Photo: Parents ACT.

Sending generic letters to parents was also a missed opportunity for both the school and the directorate to outline what might be coming for individual schools in 2027.

Ms Elliott said that information would have helped reassure parents and carers, helped them understand what equity looked like across the system, and explained why some things might look very different in their school next year.

Timely information was particularly important for children who needed support to prepare for changes in teachers, routines or learning arrangements.

“ACT parents expect there’ll be a range of different changes that might be happening in schools across the ACT next year, and it’s really difficult for parents and carers to have confidence in what those changes will be without knowing what that looks like for their school,” she said.

“We’ve got principals carrying responsibility for system decisions, and parents and carers want to know that when a school identifies a gap, the directorate will provide a timely and practical response so that students aren’t missing out.”

If this was about equity, families need to know what that would look like in their school, Ms Elliott said.

“It is really hard for people to understand how the system might need to change, and how inequitable the system has been for a number of years now,” she said.

Ms Elliott said the true cost of running a school and meeting student needs was still not known.

The current funding formulas and methodology were dated, including the Student Resourcing Allocation, which was based on calculations from 2016.

“We know that the student-need profile has changed significantly since then, but we don’t understand the true cost of meeting those needs in our classrooms every day,” Ms Elliott said.

What Parents ACT did not want to see was school communities fundraising to fill gaps that were a Directorate responsibility and hiding the true cost of education.

Ms Elliott said the budget announcement was made last year. P&Cs were routinely being asked to fund things that they hadn’t previously needed to or been asked to fund, for example, well-being programs and infrastructure projects.

“There are P&Cs who are asking questions about whether they should be investing in response to intervention programs, learning support, small group programs. It could be for anything, but it’s likely to be around literacy and numeracy,” she said.

ACT Parents would monitor resourcing arrangements throughout 2027, particularly whether students with disability or additional needs receive the reasonable adjustments they are entitled to.

Both the Canberra Liberals and the ACT Greens took the government to task for not publishing the funding comparisons between this year and next.

Liberal education spokesperson Elizabeth Lee said the spin could not hide the fact that some schools will be worse off.

Ms Lee said the process would only leave principals and teachers at greater risk.

“The minister should have been honest with school communities from the outset. Instead, principals have been left carrying the burden of explaining decisions they did not make.” Ms Lee said.

“The minister must immediately release the budgets for every ACT government school, including which schools will receive funding cuts, the size of those cuts, and the effect on staffing levels and programs.

“Parents, teachers and students deserve transparency.”

Greens education spokesperson Laura Nuttall said the government had botched the school budget process.

“The government must now come clean and release school-specific information to parents and guardians across Canberra and make sure schools are genuinely supported as they deal with the government’s cuts,” she said.

canberra.title: Driver who allegedly removed mother and baby from Wagga bus ‘no longer employed’, says minister
canberra.snippet: A bus driver who allegedly told an Aboriginal family to get off a bus outside Wagga because their toddler was crying is no longer employe...
canberra.content:
18 November 2026

Join the conversation

2

Kaneesha, seen here in Sydney with daughter Audria the day before the incident, said she is feeling much better about things after the minister called her: Photos: Supplied.

A bus driver who allegedly told an Aboriginal family to get off a bus outside Wagga because their toddler was crying is no longer employed by the coach operator, according to NSW Regional Transport Minister Jenny Aitchison.

The development comes after Region reported Kaneesha Williams, her mother Tamara and 22-month-old daughter Audria were left stranded on the roadside on Coolamon Road on Sunday (15 November).

The family had travelled by train from Sydney to Wagga before boarding a connecting NSW TrainLink coach bound for Mildura, intending to get off at Griffith.

Ms Williams, 30, said the driver told them to leave because he could not concentrate while Audria was crying, and left them by the side of the road at 3:15 pm just outside Wagga.

The family was left without alternative transport and had to wait hours in the heat for Ms Williams’ grandmother to drive from Darlington Point to collect them.

Region‘s original story has been viewed more than 28,000 times and prompted an outpouring of messages from readers expressing sympathy for the family and anger over their treatment.

Minister Aitchison then phoned Ms Williams directly.

“As the Minister for Regional Transport, I’m committed to ensuring that our regional transport network is safe and reliable for anyone who needs to use it,” she told Region.

“I have spoken to Ms Williams to reiterate my strong support for her and her family.”

Kaneesha’s mother Tamara with Audria and Kaneesha in Sydney the day before the alleged bus incident.

The minister said she apologised about what she called a “completely unacceptable situation she was placed in by the bus driver”.

“It’s extremely disappointing that a mother and her young child were allegedly treated so poorly and placed at risk on a service that they had every right to use. It’s not the standard of service we accept for any of our passengers on public transport,” she said.

“Transport for NSW is currently investigating the incident, and I’m advised the bus driver is no longer employed by the coach operator.”

Ms Williams said she was now feeling much better after being devastated by what happened on Sunday.

“The minister told me that she is taking this very seriously, that it should never happen to any family again and that she’s looking at extra training for drivers,” she said.

“I appreciated that she called me. She was on the phone with me for quite a while.”

The Darlington Point woman said her main aim in speaking publicly about her experience was to make sure something like this never happened again.

“We were lucky I had my nanna to come and pick us up, but another family might have been stranded with no options,” she said.

Ms Williams said she did not yet know whether the family would receive a refund for their bus fares or compensation for the cost of having her grandmother make the return trip from Darlington Point to collect them.

Transport for NSW is continuing to investigate the incident. It said the coach was operated by the company Dyson, which has been contacted by Region for comment.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

australia.title: Australian reader callout: tell us about your experience with insurance companies
australia.snippet: Have you been affected by rising premiums or reduced coverage? Have you had to change your provider or had difficulty making a claim? Sha...
australia.content:
Insurance premiums have risen by twice the rate of overall inflation over the past five years, putting strain on households. We’ve heard some people have had to give up on insurance altogether.

We would like to hear from people about their recent experience with insurers, across all different products such as car insurance, home and contents insurance, and health insurance.

We’d like to know how much you’ve been asked to pay for insurance in recent years, whether you’ve had to shop around, downgrade or even forgo your coverage because of the cost, and whether you’re concerned you’re now underinsured as a result.

Have you had any issues with your insurer, including if you’ve tried to negotiate on your premium? And has your insurer explained to you why your premium has gone up?

We’d also like to learn whether you’ve had trouble accessing insurance for other reasons, such as where you live or if you’ve been previously involved in a natural disaster.

And do you have any ideas for what the government, and the insurance companies, should do differently?

Please share your story using the form below if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.

australia.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
australia.snippet: Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas suppl...
australia.content:
The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.

The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.

Analysis by London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.

InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.

“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.

“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”

InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.

That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.

For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.

Of those members assessed, 69% backed stronger climate policies than the BCA, a gap that widened to 78% on energy transition issues.

Herring said the BCA does not disclose who sits on its internal climate and energy committees, obscuring how its policy positions are formed.

“We obviously do know who’s on the association board, but beyond that, there’s no transparency around those internal committees,” he said.

A spokesperson for the BCA said the association supported the “national goal of achieving net zero by 2050 and the setting of interim targets, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy and ensuring we don’t undermine our international competitiveness along the way”.

“The BCA has long advocated for gas as an essential part of the net zero transition – ensuring grid stability – while we move to greater reliance on renewable energy,” the spokesperson said.

The BCA declined to comment on the makeup of its climate and energy committee.

‘Technology agnostic’

The analysis comes as industry groups ramp up lobbying over the “safeguard mechanism”, Australia’s main policy for curbing emissions from its largest industrial facilities, which is under federal review.

While the BCA and most big resources companies publicly support the Paris agreement and Australia’s net zero 2050 carbon emissions target, they interpret what those commitments require in radically different ways to what is widely regarded as climate best practice.

Several oil and gas producer members, including Woodside, argue that increased gas supply is required to support the shift to renewables and enhance energy security in language that has been adopted by the BCA.

This rubs against those BCA members aligned with the findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which found greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure were more than enough to push the world beyond its climate goals.

InfluenceMap also found that the business council frequently lobbies for a “technology-neutral” or “technology agnostic” energy transition, which is the same language used by the fossil fuel sector designed to steer renewable energy funding toward gas.

Persephone Fraser, the ethical research and climate policy lead at fund manager Australian Ethical, said misaligned lobbying was a significant risk for companies and their shareholders, and a major risk to the economy.

“Companies must be scrutinising what is being advocated for in their name and actively correcting the record when it is inconsistent with their own positions, and interests,” Fraser said.

“Membership of an industry association cannot mean outsourcing responsibility for climate lobbying.”

Do you know more? Contact jonathan.barrett@theguardian.com

australia.title: Does Australia really have the world’s second most generous refugee scheme?
australia.snippet: One Nation wants to slash the program by 90%. But OECD data shows several countries rank higher and critics say it betrays Australia’s hi...
australia.content:
Pauline Hanson has claimed Australia’s refugee program is so generous it ranks second in the world only just behind Canada.

The One Nation leader used the claim on Wednesday to justify proposing the program be slashed by 90% from 20,000 places a year to just 2,000 if the minor rightwing party were to lead government.

Australia would still remain above the OECD average for places per capita, she claimed.

So, is Australia really punching “well above its weight” on the global stage when it comes to accepting refugees? Well, not quite to the level Hanson would like us to think.

What Hanson said…

At a press conference in Parliament House on Wednesday, Hanson said Australia had taken its share of refugees but it was now time to rein it in.

“If you look at the … only other country is Canada, and we’re second highest [behind] Canada. Even the United States only takes in 12,000. They’ve got a population of 12 times our numbers, and yet you’ve got other countries don’t even take it in whatsoever. You’ve got New Zealand’s only on 280 [per million], so we punch way above our weight,” she said.

“Our humanitarian responsibility starts here in our own country first and foremost.”

The Queensland senator said reducing the number of places from 20,000 to 2,000 in conjunction with scrapping the permanent parent visa program would save the federal budget $140bn over a decade.

Relying on an internal One Nation analysis, based on Treasury modelling and adjusted for inflation, Hanson said the lifetime cost of a humanitarian entrant was $523,000.

Doing so would still keep Australia “above the OECD average for places per capita” or at least in line with it.

The whole picture

It’s true that Australia comes in second place for the most places per capita offered to refugees processed under the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

According to its latest figures, three countries – Canada, Australia and the United States – accounted for 84% of all refugee resettlements in 2025.

But the UNHCR is not the only way the world’s refugees are resettled.

A large number of global asylum claims are processed at borders but not in Australia because of its ocean borders.

And, according to those figures as shown in a government analysis of OECD data, Australia remains in the top 10 countries offering pathways for refugees but ranks below Canada, Germany, France and even New Zealand on a per capita basis.

Under Hanson’s proposal, Australia would drop to just a fraction of the US’s reduced refugee settlement program after it was controversially suspended by US president Donald Trump.

The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said Australia’s long history of being among the top countries in the world to offer refugees a permanent home should be a source of national pride rather than a political football.

“This is about more than numbers. It is about who we are as a country. We have a choice to be mean or generous,” Jana Favero, the centre’s deputy chief executive, said.

“We all know a refugee and have a proud history over the years of welcoming people fleeing Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Ukraine, Iran, Afghanistan and former Yugoslavia. This is the Australia we love and celebrate and any other version must be rejected.”

australia.title: ‘Phantom forests’ in Australia’s arid outback used to create carbon credits meant to offset emissions, report claims
australia.snippet: Carbon credit companies reject research that found only small increase in forest and canopy cover in regeneration areas despite wet condi...
australia.content:
A fight over the legitimacy of Australia’s climate change policy has reignited after researchers claimed “phantom forests” in the semi-arid outback are being used to create offsets that allow fossil fuel companies to keep pumping out pollution.

A group of academics, including professors from the Australian National University and the University of New South Wales, said they had examined 50 forest regeneration projects used to create carbon credits.

Led by Prof Andrew Macintosh, the former federal government carbon credit scheme integrity chair and the director of ANU’s Centre for Environmental Markets, the researchers said they found only a small increase in forest and tree crown cover in the areas over the past five years despite wet conditions.

They said the conclusions were consistent with their previous peer-reviewed studies that found Australia’s method for creating carbon credits from forest regeneration was doing little to nothing to help address the climate crisis.

The research was published in a report released on Wednesday by the Australian Conservation Foundation. Prof David Eldridge, one of the report’s authors and a former principal research scientist with the NSW environment department, said he was “gobsmacked” that “phantom forests” in outback areas north-west of the remote town of Bourke could earn carbon credits for forest regrowth.

“Some of these areas have never grown forests; they will never grow forests,” he said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The findings were rejected by companies that manage what are known as human-induced regeneration projects in north-western NSW. “These are some of the most closely examined carbon projects in the country, and the evidence on the ground shows they are working,” a spokesperson for Green Collar, a business that manages carbon credit projects, said.

Each carbon credit is said to represent one tonne of emissions that has been removed from, or prevented from being released to, the atmosphere.

Their use is contentious, in part, because industrial-polluting companies that are required to cut emissions under a federal policy known as the safeguard mechanism are allowed to buy an unlimited number of credits to count as their own cuts while continuing to pollute.

Scientists have warned limiting the climate crisis requires rapid direct cuts in emissions and that carbon credits – also known as offsets – should be used sparingly.

The Australian Conservation Foundation said it showed coal and gas companies should be banned from claiming offsets as their own emissions cuts.

Adam Bandt, the foundation’s chief executive and a former Australian Greens leader, said the safeguard mechanism was meant to “cut climate pollution and protect us from big coal and gas threatening our lives and livelihoods, but it’s not working”.

“Putting more climate pollution into the atmosphere now could push us past dangerous tipping points. It can’t be offset, and the science tells us to keep coal and gas in the ground,” he said.

Macintosh said the evidence showed the projects were by and large not regenerating forest, but had created more than 60m carbon credits worth up to $2bn.

The report said the safeguard mechanism was being “materially undermined” by poor-quality credits. It said a “flood of cheap, low integrity” credits was making it cheaper in many cases for big polluters to pay for offsets rather than make direct emissions cuts.

There have been more than 430 human-induced regeneration projects in Australia since 2013, covering an area of 38m hectares – larger than Japan. The federal government is now reviewing the safeguard policy, as required under legislation.

A spokesperson for the Clean Energy Regulator, which manages the scheme, said it took allegations about the integrity or efficacy of carbon credit projects seriously, and had confidence in the forest regeneration method.

It said projects were required to demonstrate every five years that canopy cover was increasing, and it had rejected non-complying areas that could have received 6.7m carbon credits.

Green Collar said it stood “firmly behind the integrity of its human-induced regeneration projects” and expressed frustration that the report had not been publicly released or published in a peer-reviewed journal. It said the researchers had “judged these carbon projects with satellite pictures and a single field visit”.

“Carbon is stored in stems, branches, leaves, roots and dead timber. Satellite canopy products see leaves from above. They do not measure the wood and roots where most of that carbon sits,” its spokesperson said.

Skye Glenday, the chief executive of Climate Friendly, another carbon credit project developer, said the criticisms of the carbon credit projects were “at odds with the facts and the extensive independent scientific and regulatory scrutiny that is applied to all projects”.

“Debate about the use of offsets is legitimate, but let’s have that debate on its merits rather than undermining the carbon drawdown Australia also needs,” she said.

australia.title: ‘I didn’t notice his body being purple’: Byron Bay doula left newborn to inflate a jumping castle, court hears
australia.snippet: Inquest into deaths of four babies born in free births or at home in northern NSW between 2022 and 2024 hears ‘something was seriously wr...
australia.content:
Baby DH was born in an inflatable pool, in a candle-lit room in his parents’ home near Byron Bay, with no one medically trained present. There are two very different versions of what happened next.

In the parents’ version, the doula reassured them Baby DH was OK, then left to inflate a jumping castle while their newborn turned purple, became floppy, and struggled to breathe. In the doula’s version, everything seemed OK but she suggested they seek more help if they wanted to.

The New South Wales coroner’s court heard the two competing narratives on Wednesday as part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births.

The babies died in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

Baby DH lived for just over eight hours.

“The evidence will be that from his first minutes of life, [Baby DH] showed signs that something was seriously wrong,” the Lismore courtroom heard.

“His parents saw those signs. They raised them again and again with their doula, who they had engaged to watch for exactly that. Their doula, in this case, was a woman named Amy Lou Smith.

“Each time the parents raised their concerns, they were reassured by Amy Lou. An ambulance was not called until moments before [Baby DH] stopped breathing.”

His father described the baby as floppy after birth. “His colour, his whole body was purple with his hands and feet darker still,” the court heard, and Smith told them some purple in the hands and feet was normal.

“I didn’t notice his body being purple,” Smith told the court.

Told the baby’s colour wasn’t improving, Smith said “as long as his abdomen isn’t purple”, according to evidence from the parents. The mother was shocked. His whole body had been purple all along. His temperature was low, 34.5C. Smith suggested trying to get it up to 37C.

“I believed if they had real concerns, that they would call an ambulance and not be texting a non medically trained doula,” Smith told the court.

Smith, the inquest heard, described his laboured breathing as “cute little noises”. “I didn’t say that,” Smith told the court.

The court heard Smith told the couple Baby DH would have been put on oxygen if he was in hospital. But Smith later told the court she didn’t know what the hospital would have done.

He had strange lumps on his body, and wasn’t feeding. Smith suggested they get the lumps checked out, and warned that babies sometimes take a while to latch on to the breast, according to the parents’ evidence.

The court heard Smith left to set up a jumping castle for her son’s birthday. She sent the couple a picture of the castle later, as they were trying to contact a doctor, the court heard.

Smith told the court the castle was already set up, and the couple was happy for her to leave.

“Everything felt like it was OK,” she said.

Eventually, the parents spoke to the GP they had tried to contact earlier. The GP told them to call triple zero. They did, and did CPR until the paramedics got there. But Baby DH was declared dead at the hospital.

After the father had made the emergency call, Smith also told them to call an ambulance, and sent them instructions on infant CPR.

Throughout the hearing, Smith denied that any of her advice or comments constituted clinical advice.

Neonatologist Dr Paul Evans, the court heard, had found Baby DH had a complex heart defect, one that would have shown up on an X-ray. The baby could have been treated, and a birth plan with proximity to a major hospital and specialist cardiac care prepared, the court heard.

The child’s death was not inevitable, Evans found.

While pregnant, Baby DH’s mother decided to rely on a doula. She first approached a woman the court heard was likely to be Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper who was also involved in the care of another baby previously mentioned during the inquest. But Kali didn’t feel she could help, so they turned to Smith.

The court heard the couple paid for an online “sovereign birth course” for Smith and was reassured that she had enough experience. They agreed on an emergency plan.

Smith, who became a birth doula in 2020, was quizzed on her experience in court.

She has a degree in fine art and has worked as a social worker and a youth worker.

She told the court she is not medically trained in any way but did an online “full-spectrum doula course”. She learned CPR but was not familiar with how to apply it to a newborn – she denied she had given the parents the impression she was.

She had no training about a newborn’s colour, breathing, or feeding, but she did go to a retreat where she learned about referring a woman to more support if needed.

She had been present at 15 births over four years, nine alongside a midwife, and conceded she didn’t know what a low-risk birth would look like. She had read a couple of books about birthing, but they were more “spiritual”, the court heard.

She agreed that she now believes the best model of care for a home birth is for a clinically trained midwife to work alongside a doula.

The inquest continues.

world.title: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
world.snippet: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose ...
world.content:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

world.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
world.snippet: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been a...
world.content:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

world.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
world.snippet: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member ...
world.content:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

world.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
world.snippet: Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria An American basketball player has been arrested i...
world.content:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

world.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
world.snippet: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The ...
world.content:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”
